items.title: AI and your job: Threat or opportunity?
items.summary:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - Artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of everyday life, raising questions about what the technology could mean for workers and their jobs.

Some economists believe AI poses a particular threat to entry-level and repetitive work, including call center, data entry and junior copywriting jobs, according to The Wall Street Journal. Those tasks may be easier to automate. [...] But AI could also create opportunities. A Bloomberg article points to potential job growth in construction and manufacturing as companies build data centers and produce the chips that power the technology. Some higher-skilled office workers could also benefit if AI helps them become more productive. [...] The long-term impact on jobs remains unclear, but workers can take steps to prepare. Exploring AI chatbots, writing assistants and other tools may help people find ways to work more efficiently and develop skills that complement the technology.

items.title: Opinion: AI cannot replace being human – The Battalion
items.summary: I understand the appeal. College is busy. Between classes, jobs, extracurriculars, leadership positions and trying to maintain some semblance of a social life, there are never enough hours in the day. AI makes things easier. It can generate an outline, rewrite a paragraph, summarize a reading or produce an entire essay before you have even finished your Celsius. But convenience does not necessarily facilitate education. [...] There is also something to be said about individuality. AI can generate an argument, imitate a writing style or suggest a creative direction, but our perspectives are developed through our own experiences, disagreements, mistakes and interpretations. The things that make our voices interesting are often the very things that cannot be neatly generated from a prompt. If we constantly rely on the same tools to tell us what to think and how to express it, we risk losing the differences that make [...] I am not asking anyone to abandon AI. I use it, and I recognize the benefits it provides. But I do think we need to become more conscientious about when we use it and what we are asking it to do for us. Let it help with the tedious tasks. Let it serve as a resource. But do not let it become a substitute for your own intellectual development.

items.title: ‘AI rebounding’: Nearly 20% of U.S. workers replaced by AI are being asked back | Fortune
items.summary:
Ford also hired and promoted 350 experienced engineers in June after AI-powered quality control tools failed to perform as expected. The automaker said AI had contributed to quality improvements but emphasized the importance of combining the tech with experienced engineering teams. [...] “Organizations are making fast, sometimes myopic, decisions about their people based on an incomplete picture of what their employees can do with or without AI,” Lucy Beaumont, global senior vice president of product and design at SHL, said in a press release. “AI rebounding is what happens when a company automates a role before it has genuinely assessed the human capability inside it. items.title: Military-made AI tool helped thwart World Cup bomb threat - Federal News Network
items.summary:
The 2026 World Cup brought more than six million spectators from around the world to more than 100 matches in 16 host cities in the U.S., Canada and Mexico over the course of two months, prompting a massive interagency effort to secure those sites using technologies like AI and drones. Two people were charged in connection with another bomb threat against FIFA during a World Cup match at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. [...] A military-made artificial intelligence tool helped law enforcement thwart a bomb threat at the FIFA World Cup in California this summer.

The previously undisclosed incident occurred June 18, when Switzerland faced Bosnia and Herzegovina at SoFi Stadium outside Los Angeles, Army Capt. Ryan Hetrick, who leads the Pentagon’s Generative AI Task Force, said Nov. 6 at an AI event in Washington. [...] Hetrick has become one of the military’s biggest — and busiest — evangelists for AI. The GenAI Task Force travels around the globe to sit down with troops on operations floors and in the field and find AI fixes for their most pressing problems.

items.title: Recent advances in AI are creating a 'paradigm shift' for robotics - Berkeley News
items.summary: Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] “Robots are advancing quickly, but developing them for real-world environments remains slow, data-intensive and difficult to scale,” Huang said. “Working with UC Berkeley, NVIDIA is helping advance a new approach combining agentic AI, simulation and open industrial task-focused benchmarks to help developers rapidly test and improve robot behavior before deployment.” [...] Earlier this year, he and his team began experimenting with a change to the way the robot code is organized. Using a framework they called Graph-as-Policy, robot tasks are segmented into individual skills, such as finding an object, planning a grasp and moving the gripper without collisions. Goldberg likened it to individual building blocks that fit together into something much larger.

items.title: FDA seeks input on telesurgery, autonomous robotics
items.summary:
In another example of teleoperation, manufacturers are developing devices that enable technicians to remotely perform ultrasounds, the FDA said. Robotic devices include stereotactic navigation systems, imaging devices and endoluminal navigation devices. [...] Rapid advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning and connectivity are driving expansion of robotic applications in a wide range of clinical settings, the FDA said. Increases in processing power, data storage and computational efficiency are enabling progress in robotic systems with autonomous capabilities. [...] Incorporating autonomy into robotic systems could support procedural accuracy, reproducibility or workflow efficiency and potentially improve clinical outcomes, the FDA said. However, distinct risks such as incorrect autonomous execution, reduced user vigilance and limited adaptability to procedural variability may accompany the potential benefits.

items.title: Google Releases Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics Control, Simulation, and Policy Improvement - InfoQ
items.summary:
Specialized vision-language-action systems such as OpenVLA-class policies, Physical Intelligence's π-family models, and NVIDIA GR00T with Isaac-oriented tooling optimize for action prediction under robot embodiments and typically rely on large teleoperation or simulation corpora. Scene-to-sim and generative world tools, World Labs-style reconstructions, NVIDIA DreamDojo-style action video, and Isaac Sim digital twins, emphasize environment synthesis or video prediction without necessarily [...] In the published prompts, Argon directs a Boston Dynamics Spot through a foot-pedal task after practice in a MuJoCo twin, steers a simpler arm with visual coordinates and HTTP motion primitives, and closes a loop with the Gemini Omni video world model. Real2Sim examples rebuild MuJoCo scenes from teleoperation video; labeling prompts annotate demonstration footage for behavior cloning. Google also reports synthesizing domain-randomized MuJoCo episodes from one RGB photo to fine-tune a [...] Early practitioner reaction focused on simulation fidelity. Davin YC Dong commented on X:

> Google's Argon robotics examples tune simulation twins against contact events as well as visuals. That is the part I'd inspect: a scene can look convincing while its objects behave incorrectly. For manipulation, matching what happens at contact matters as much as matching pixels.

items.title: Autonomous EV developer Humble Robotics adds $51M to expand - TT
items.summary:
“We’ve spent years proving that a truck can drive itself. The harder question is how to make autonomy something a freight operator can depend on every day,” founder and CEO Eyal Cohen said.

PERSPECTIVE: From proving autonomy works to proving it scales

---

The financing comes six months after the San Francisco-based company emerged from stealth with the Humble Hauler, a battery-electric, cabless Class 8 autonomous vehicle. Humble previously raised $24 million in seed funding led by Eclipse. [...] The Hauler uses vision-language-action models and is equipped with cameras, lidar and radar that provide 360-degree coverage of its surroundings. The battery-electric skateboard platform has an aerodynamic shield at the front, while shipping containers can be attached through a twist-lock interface. [...] Humble Robotics raised $51 million in Series A financing, bringing its total funding to $75 million less than a year after its founding.
 The company is developing the Humble Hauler, a battery-electric, cabless Class 8 autonomous vehicle for regional freight routes under 250 miles.
 Humble will fund customer pilots, testing, early manufacturing and expansion into vehicles for 40-foot containers and 53-foot dry van and refrigerated trailers.
